attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post. He is not quoting anyone else.

semantics.note: The proposition matches the sentence, and it correctly marks 'arguably' as a hedge on the 'almost none' clause. The firm part is polemical, but it can be read as an observation about what evidence Vance had on the speech date.

contract.note: The contract reads 'doesn't have any evidence' as being about what Vance possessed, not only what he cited. That is a fair, ordinary reading of the words. The result depends on that reading and on 'excessive', which has no stated standard. The contract rightly gives the hedged scarcity clause no weight.

evidence.note: The official transcript is correctly dated. The burdens Vance cites are European (GDPR, DSA), not US. This fits the narrow 'presented no evidence' reading, but the speech cannot show everything Vance possessed.

A preprint available before the speech that criticises the audit metric required by NYC Local Law 144. It argues the rule is flawed, not excessive, and nothing links it to Vance. It does not meet the contradiction condition.

reviews.rationale: The speech cites only EU burdens, but the contract says failing to cite evidence in one speech is not enough to support the claim. Nothing in the packet records the full basis for Vance's view. The one possible counterexample (a critique of an NYC audit rule) does not argue the rule is excessive and is not tied to Vance. The packet settles neither the support condition nor the contradiction condition.
